summary: Defines MIBs for performing ping, traceroute and lookup operations at a remote host. When managing a network, it is useful to start these operations on another machine and retrieve the results. The lookup capability helps map names or addresses. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of testing the road from your own house, you ask a friend across town to test it and report back. This lets a management tool do that with ping and traceroute.

questions: how to run ping remotely with snmp
what is the remote ping mib
how to run traceroute remotely with snmp
subtitle: SNMP tables that let a management station tell a remote device to run ping, traceroute and name lookups and report back.

tldr.problem: Network managers often need ping and traceroute results measured from a remote host, but each vendor offered its own enterprise-specific MIB for it, so tools could not interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: Three SMIv2 MIB modules (DISMAN-PING-MIB, DISMAN-TRACEROUTE-MIB and DISMAN-NSLOOKUP-MIB) let a management station create a table row over SNMP, which starts the operation at the managed node, and then read the results from result tables.
tldr.outcome: It gives a standards-based way to run these tests remotely, replaces RFC 2925, and warns that the functions can be misused to attack other systems.

today: RFC 4560 is a Proposed Standard from June 2006. It obsoletes RFC 2925, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Ping, Traceroute and Lookup
sections.content:
Ping and traceroute are two very useful functions for managing networks. Ping is typically used to find out whether a path exists between two hosts, while traceroute shows an actual path. Both yield round-trip times in milliseconds, which are a rough approximation of network transit time. The lookup function is the equivalent of name-to-address calls such as gethostbyname() and getaddrinfo(), and of address-to-name calls such as gethostbyaddr() and getnameinfo().

Ping is usually built on the ICMP Echo facility, but it can also use the UDP echo port (7), time an SNMP query, or time a TCP connect attempt. Different methods give different response times, so a management application needs to know which one is used. It is RECOMMENDED that the ping here use ICMP Echo.

Traceroute sends probe packets with increasing time-to-live values. Each hop rejects the probe until its TTL is large enough and returns an ICMP message that reveals the hop and its round-trip time. Implementations SHOULD use UDP packets to a hopefully unused port, and SHOULD NOT use ICMP Echo Request probes, because routers may refuse to send TTL-expired messages about ICMP packets, which makes hops invisible.

The abstract notes the motivation: several enterprise-specific MIBs for remote ping or traceroute already existed, and this memo defines a standards-based solution to enable interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Ping asks "are you there, and how fast do you answer?" Traceroute lists every stop along the way, and lookup finds the name that goes with a number, or the number that goes with a name.

sections.title: How Remote Operations Work
sections.content:
Three roles are involved. The management station is the local host that starts the operation with an SNMP request. The managed node is a remote host that implements these MIBs; it receives the request over SNMP and performs the actual ping, traceroute or lookup. The target host is the machine being tested. The management station later receives the result of the operation from the managed node.

The RFC defines three MIB modules: DISMAN-PING-MIB, DISMAN-TRACEROUTE-MIB and DISMAN-NSLOOKUP-MIB. The modules follow the Internet-Standard Management Framework and are written in SMIv2. The ping and traceroute MIBs can set up tests that repeat periodically and generate notifications about results, which the RFC compares to shell scripts that administrators wrote in the past.
sections.plainLanguage: You are the boss in an office. You tell a worker in another city to test a road, the worker does it, and then tells you what happened.

sections.title: The Ping MIB
sections.content:
A test lives in a row of the pingCtlTable. A test starts when pingCtlAdminStatus is set to enabled(1), after the row exists and its pingCtlRowStatus is active(1). A single SNMP PDU can create and start a test by setting the target address, the admin status and the row status to createAndGo(4). Setting the row status to destroy(6) deletes an active request.

Rows are indexed by pingCtlOwnerIndex, a SnmpAdminString that lets the SNMPv3 View-Based Access Control Model identify a user's entries, and by pingCtlTestName, which lets one application have several tests outstanding.

Key settings include pingCtlDataSize (default 0 octets, up to 65507), pingCtlTimeOut (1 to 60 seconds, default 3), and pingCtlProbeCount (1 to 15 probes, default 1). With maximum values a single test can take at most 15 minutes. With defaults it takes at most 3 seconds.

Results go in the pingResultsTable, one entry per started test, and past probes go in the pingProbeHistoryTable. The number of history rows per test is limited by pingCtlMaxRows (default 50); when the limit is reached the oldest entry is removed. History index values MUST start at 1 and wrap after the maximum. Notifications defined are pingProbeFailed, pingTestFailed and pingTestCompleted. The probe method is chosen by pingCtlType, with ICMP echo as the default, plus UDP echo, SNMP query and TCP connection attempt as other values.
sections.plainLanguage: You fill in a request card with who to ping, how long to wait and how many tries. Once the card is active the device starts pinging and writes the answers on a results sheet.

sections.title: The Traceroute MIB
sections.content:
The traceroute module has the same shape as the ping module, with a traceRouteCtlTable for requests, a traceRouteResultsTable, a traceRouteProbeHistoryTable and a traceRouteHopsTable that can store the current path, one entry per hop, when traceRouteCtlCreateHopsEntries is true. Tests are started and deleted in the same way as ping tests.

Defaults for a request include a timeout of 3 seconds, 3 probes per hop (traceRouteCtlProbesPerHop), UDP port 33434 (traceRouteCtlPort, the IANA assigned traceroute port), a maximum TTL of 30 (traceRouteCtlMaxTtl), an initial TTL of 1 and a maximum of 5 consecutive timeouts (traceRouteCtlMaxFailures). The function ends when the maximum TTL is exceeded or the target is reached.

Worst-case timing can be long. The theoretical maximum is 42 hours and 30 minutes, the product of timeout, probes per hop and maximum TTL, which the RFC calls clearly too long to wait. The defaults give at most 4 minutes and 30 seconds. Agents are RECOMMENDED to impose a time limit, and the max-failures object throttles how long traceroute keeps raising the TTL without getting any response.

Notifications are traceRoutePathChange, traceRouteTestFailed and traceRouteTestCompleted.
sections.plainLanguage: Traceroute is like asking a letter to report in at every post office it passes. You can set how long to wait at each stop and when to give up.

sections.title: The Lookup MIB
sections.content:
A lookup is started by an SNMP set on lookupCtlRowStatus. The type of address in lookupCtlTargetAddressType picks the function. The value dns(16) means a name should be turned into numeric addresses, as getaddrinfo() or gethostbyname() does. The values ipv4(1) or ipv6(2) mean an address should be turned into names, as getnameinfo() or gethostbyaddr() does. lookupCtlOperStatus reports enabled(1), notStarted(2) or completed(3).

Results go in the lookupResultsTable, with a third index, lookupResultsIndex, so one request can have many answers, because a remote host can be multi-homed or have several names. Answers are stored in the order retrieved starting at index 1. When a reverse lookup identifies an official host name, it MUST get index 1. Results may differ from a pure DNS lookup because they can be influenced by local tables and other sources.

lookupPurgeTime automatically deletes finished requests and their results after a delay. The default is 900 seconds (15 minutes), up to 86400, and 0 disables deletion. lookupMaxConcurrentRequests defaults to 10. An implementation SHOULD NOT keep SNMP-created result entries across agent restarts.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a phone book question asked by someone else. Give a name and get numbers back, or give a number and get names back.

sections.title: Conformance Levels
sections.content:
Each of the three modules has two current compliance statements: full and minimum. The minimum statements are meant for devices with very limited resources. The main difference is that minimum compliance does not require dynamic creation and deletion of table entries, while full compliance does.

If a device does not support row creation, at least one entry in the control table MUST already exist when the agent starts offering the module. Ping and traceroute also keep a deprecated compliance statement that was current in RFC 2925. The new full statements are semantically identical to the deprecated ones, but some object groups had to be split to allow the minimal statements.
sections.plainLanguage: Big devices can do everything on the list. Tiny devices may do a smaller version, such as showing one ready-made test instead of letting you create new ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Many objects are read-write or read-create, and setting them in an unprotected environment can harm network operations. Unauthorized access to the concurrency limits can overload the managed node. Unauthorized access to the control tables can disturb measurements and can be misused for illegal data retrieval, or to attack other systems with floods of ping probes, traceroute probes or lookup requests. In insecure environments the RFC says it is RECOMMENDED that these MIBs not be supported.

Setting lookupPurgeTime to 0 or near 0 can delete results before they are read, while very high values can use many resources. Readable objects can also be sensitive, so GET and notification access needs control, and values may need encryption in transit.

Owner indexes let the View-Based Access Control Model (VACM) give each user access to only their own rows. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. It is RECOMMENDED that implementers consider SNMPv3 with its cryptographic mechanisms, and deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting strangers press the ping button is like letting them ring your doorbell nonstop. So only trusted people should get the remote control.
